item.title: US weighs lifting sanctions on Iran's 'shadow fleet' to address surging costs
item.description:
US weighs lifting sanctions on Iran's 'shadow fleet' to address surging costs

The US is considering lifting sanctions on “shadow fleet” tankers tied to Russia and Iran to address soaring diesel prices ahead of midterm elections, according to multiple reports and a senior US official.

US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in a video address to an energy forum in Riyadh this week that the Trump administration was discussing easing sanctions on shadow fleet vessels to address record freight rates that have driven up costs of shipping American energy abroad, Energy Aspects, a research group, said.

The Financial Times reported on Thursday that the US could allow the sale of blacklisted vessels to non-sanctioned operators and lift sanctions, allowing them to operate without restrictions.

Reuters reported the US could allow “legal oil" to flow on previously sanctioned vessels, effectively allowing sanctioned ships to carry crude or petroleum products not sanctioned by the US.

Iran’s shadow fleet rose in full force in 2018, after the US unilaterally withdrew from a nuclear agreement with Iran and global powers, officially titled the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action. The US imposed debilitating sanctions on Iran and has honed in on its oil industry.

Energy Aspects estimates that around 15 percent of the world's tanker fleet is under US sanctions.

Read more: US weighs lifting sanctions on Iran's 'shadow fleet' to address surging costs

item.title: Hormuz controlled by US and allies, not Iran: Centcom chief
item.description:
Hormuz controlled by US and allies, not Iran: Centcom chief

The Strait of Hormuz "is controlled by the United States and our regional partners, not Iran", the head of US Central Command (Centcom) has said.

In a video statement, Centcom commander Brad Cooper said the US blockade of Iranian ports had imposed "a devastating cost" on the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

He said it had completely halted Iran's maritime exports and imports, "with the exception of humanitarian assistance we have allowed in".

Cooper said the US had "prevented Iran from exporting at least 25 billion dollars worth of crude oil" and had "significantly degraded Iran's ability to project power far beyond its borders".

He added that US forces had helped Gulf allies ship more than 100 million barrels of crude through the strait in the past week, with around 400 merchant vessels passing through.

In total, the US had helped regional partners move 1.3 billion barrels through Hormuz in recent months, he said.

item.title: Saudi Arabia says Houthi attacks violate terms of rapprochement with Iran
item.description:
Saudi Arabia says Houthi attacks violate terms of rapprochement with Iran

Saudi Arabia has publicly accused Iran of encouraging Yemen's Houthis to attack the kingdom, saying it violates a 2023 diplomatic deal it reached with Tehran to smooth over relations.

"We think the escalation by the Houthis at this later stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran," Rayed Krimly, deputy minister for public diplomacy at the foreign ministry, told journalists on Friday, in a rare public statement.

Krimly’s comments mark the first public signal that the war in Yemen has put pressure on Riyadh’s ties to Tehran.

Krimly said that the Houthis’ attacks were a breach of a March 2023 rapprochement that was brokered by China under which Saudi Arabia and Iran resumed diplomatic relations.

At the time, the agreement was seen as a sign of China’s successful foreign policy. Beijing has good ties with both Tehran and Riyadh.

“[Iran] continues to arm, train and support the Houthi militia in violation of relevant UN Security Council resolutions and in violation of its commitments in the Beijing agreement,” Krimly said.

The agreement was generally understood to include a commitment from Tehran to restrain the Houthis in support of a United Nations-backed ceasefire.

Read more: Saudi Arabia says Houthi attacks violate terms of rapprochement with Iran

item.title: Saudi Arabia to execute man for being at protests and funerals when he was 15
item.description:
Use of death penalty against people for crimes committed when they were children a ‘new low’, say rights groups

A young man faces imminent execution in Saudi Arabia for attending protests and funerals when he was aged 15 to 17, say human rights groups, in the latest example of the kingdom’s surging use of the death penalty for non-violent crimes.

Youssef al-Manasif was arrested in 2017 and accused of crimes including joining demonstrations for religious freedom by the Shia minority and attending funerals that the Saudi authorities deem to be protests. He was convicted and sentenced to death by the specialised criminal court, a secretive tribunal set up for terrorism-related cases.

item.description:

  • Food and fuel run low as besieged Yemeni city braces for Houthi breakthrough

The future of western security is being fought out in the mountains and hills surrounding the south-western Yemeni city of Taiz, the country’s former prime minster has said.

Maeen Abdulmalik Saeed, now an adviser to Yemen’s president, said it would be catastrophic if the city fell to the Iran-backed Houthi rebels, since control of the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait in the Red Sea and the road to Aden – the site of the UN-recognised government – would be lost.
